name: SQL
title: SQL: asking questions of a database
intro: SQL (Structured Query Language) is how programs talk to relational databases, which keep data in tables of rows and columns. It came out of IBM research in the 1970s and is still everywhere: banks, shops, phones and web sites all store their data in databases you query with SQL. It is different from the other languages here: you don't write the steps, you describe the result you want, and the database works out how to get it. These lessons use SQLite, a small database that lives in a single file and is built into Python, every phone and every web browser; the SQL itself is close to what PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server accept. All examples share the sample database from the first lesson, and each one starts from a fresh copy, so changes made in one example don't carry over. Results are shown as a header line and then one line per row. To try them yourself, install the sqlite3 program, paste the setup from the first lesson, then type the queries.

lessons.title: Tables and SELECT
lessons.summary: The sample database, SELECT, columns and expressions.

sections.p: A database holds tables. Each table has named columns, each with a type, and any number of rows. Here is the sample database every lesson uses: a table of trees, a table of squirrels (each living in one tree), and a table of the nuts each squirrel has buried. PRIMARY KEY marks the column that identifies a row, and REFERENCES says a column holds the key of a row in another table. You don't need to type this in to follow the lessons; it is here so you know what the tables hold.

SELECT asks for columns FROM a table. * means every column. Keywords are often written in capitals so they stand out, but SQL doesn't mind either way. A statement ends with a semicolon. NULL means no value: the ash tree's height was never measured.
sections.code: SELECT * FROM trees;
sections.out:
id | kind | height_m
1 | oak | 21.5
2 | hazel | 6.0
3 | beech | 30.0
4 | ash | NULL

sections.p: List the columns you want, separated by commas. A column can also be an expression, and AS gives it a name in the result. || joins strings in SQL, and functions like UPPER and LENGTH work on each row.
sections.code:
SELECT name, 2026 - born AS age, UPPER(name) || '!' AS shout
FROM squirrels;
sections.out:
name | age | shout
Hazel | 4 | HAZEL!
Acorn | 2 | ACORN!
Bramble | 5 | BRAMBLE!
Pip | 1 | PIP!
Rowan | 3 | ROWAN!

practice.code: SELECT kind, height_m * 2 AS double FROM trees WHERE id = 2;
practice.why: Only the row with id 2 is chosen, and the second column is the height times two, named double.

practice.q: What does NULL mean in a table?
practice.why: NULL is not 0 or '': it means the value is missing or unknown, which is why it needs its own tests.

lessons.title: Filtering and sorting
lessons.summary: WHERE, AND/OR, IN, LIKE, IS NULL, ORDER BY and LIMIT.

sections.p: WHERE keeps only the rows where a condition is true. Compare with =, <> (not equal), < and >, and combine with AND, OR and NOT. IN (...) checks against a list, and LIKE matches a pattern where % stands for any run of characters.
sections.out:
name | born
Hazel | 2022
Acorn | 2024
Rowan | 2023

nut | count
hazelnut | 5
beechnut | 20
beechnut | 4

sections.p: Comparing anything with NULL gives neither true nor false but NULL, so height_m = NULL never matches. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. COALESCE gives the first value that isn't NULL, which is handy for a fallback.
sections.out:
kind

kind
ash

name | home
Pip | 2
Rowan | homeless

sections.p: Rows come back in no promised order unless you ask for one. ORDER BY sorts by one or more columns, DESC from largest to smallest. LIMIT keeps only the first few rows, so together they answer questions like "the three biggest".
sections.out:
nut | count
beechnut | 20
acorn | 12
acorn | 7

name
Bramble
Hazel
Rowan
Acorn
Pip

practice.why: Hazel and Acorn live in tree 1 and Pip was born in 2025. ORDER BY name puts them in alphabetical order.

practice.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM squirrels WHERE tree_id <> 1;
practice.why: Bramble (tree 3) and Pip (tree 2) match. Rowan's tree_id is NULL, and NULL <> 1 is not true, so Rowan is left out.

lessons.title: Counting and grouping
lessons.summary: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, GROUP BY and HAVING.

sections.p: Aggregate functions turn many rows into one value: COUNT(*) counts rows, and SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX work on a column. Without grouping, the whole table becomes a single result row. Aggregates skip NULLs, which is why AVG(height_m) averages three trees, not four.
sections.out:
stashes | nuts | biggest
7 | 53 | 20

trees | measured | avg_height
4 | 3 | 19.2

sections.p: GROUP BY splits the rows into groups that share a value, and the aggregates are worked out once per group. Every column you select should either be in the GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate.
sections.code:
SELECT nut, COUNT(*) AS stashes, SUM(count) AS total
FROM stashes
GROUP BY nut
ORDER BY total DESC;
sections.out:
nut | stashes | total
beechnut | 2 | 24
acorn | 3 | 22
hazelnut | 2 | 7

sections.p: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups afterwards, so it can test an aggregate. The order of the clauses is fixed: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
sections.code:
SELECT squirrel_id, SUM(count) AS total
FROM stashes
WHERE buried_on >= '2026-10-01'
GROUP BY squirrel_id
HAVING SUM(count) > 5
ORDER BY squirrel_id;
sections.out:
squirrel_id | total
1 | 21
3 | 7

practice.code:
SELECT squirrel_id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM stashes
GROUP BY squirrel_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY squirrel_id;
practice.why: Squirrel 1 has three stashes and squirrel 3 has two. Squirrels 2 and 4 have one each and are filtered out by HAVING.
WHERE runs on single rows before the groups exist, so it can't use an aggregate.

lessons.title: Joining tables
lessons.summary: JOIN ... ON, table aliases and LEFT JOIN.

sections.p: Keeping each fact in one place means the answer to a question is often spread over several tables. A JOIN pairs rows from two tables that match an ON condition, usually a key in one equal to a reference in the other. Short aliases such as s and t keep the column names readable.
sections.code:
SELECT s.name, t.kind AS tree
FROM squirrels AS s
JOIN trees AS t ON t.id = s.tree_id
ORDER BY s.name;
sections.out:
name | tree
Acorn | oak
Bramble | beech
Hazel | oak
Pip | hazel

sections.p: A plain JOIN drops rows that have no match, which is why Rowan, who has no tree, is missing above. LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with NULL when nothing matches. It is the way to find things that are missing, such as trees nobody lives in.
sections.code:
SELECT t.kind, COUNT(s.id) AS residents
FROM trees AS t
LEFT JOIN squirrels AS s ON s.tree_id = t.id
GROUP BY t.id
ORDER BY t.id;
sections.out:
kind | residents
oak | 2
hazel | 1
beech | 1
ash | 0

sections.p: Joins chain: each new JOIN adds another table to the rows built so far. Here every stash is joined to its squirrel and that squirrel's tree, then grouped to total the nuts stored at each tree.
sections.code:
SELECT t.kind AS tree, SUM(st.count) AS nuts
FROM stashes AS st
JOIN squirrels AS s ON s.id = st.squirrel_id
JOIN trees AS t ON t.id = s.tree_id
GROUP BY t.kind
ORDER BY nuts DESC;
sections.out:
tree | nuts
beech | 27
oak | 24
hazel | 2

practice.code:
SELECT s.name
FROM squirrels AS s
LEFT JOIN stashes AS st ON st.squirrel_id = s.id
WHERE st.id IS NULL;
practice.why: Rowan has no stashes, so the LEFT JOIN fills the stash columns with NULL, and the WHERE keeps exactly those rows.

practice.q: Why does a plain JOIN of squirrels and trees leave out Rowan?
options: Rowan's tree_id is NULL, so no tree matches
practice.answer: Rowan's tree_id is NULL, so no tree matches
practice.why: An inner JOIN keeps only pairs that satisfy ON. LEFT JOIN would keep Rowan with NULL tree columns.

lessons.title: Changing data
lessons.summary: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and constraints that refuse bad data.

sections.p: INSERT INTO ... VALUES adds rows, UPDATE ... SET changes them and DELETE FROM removes them. UPDATE and DELETE without a WHERE change every row in the table, so always write the WHERE first. The example ends with a SELECT to show the result.
sections.out:
name | tree_id
Nutmeg | 4

nut | count
acorn | 12
hazelnut | 15
beechnut | 20
acorn | 7
hazelnut | 12

sections.p: The table definitions from the first lesson include rules: NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK (count > 0). The database refuses any change that breaks one, so bad data can't get in whichever program is writing. Here the first insert is refused because a squirrel called Hazel already exists, and nothing after the error runs.
sections.out:
before
5

practice.code:
UPDATE trees SET height_m = 8.5 WHERE kind = 'ash';
SELECT COUNT(*) AS measured FROM trees WHERE height_m IS NOT NULL;
practice.why: The ash was the only tree without a height. After the UPDATE all four are measured.

practice.q: What does  DELETE FROM stashes;  do?
practice.why: Without WHERE, every row matches. DROP TABLE is the statement that removes the table itself.

lessons.title: Subqueries and WITH
lessons.summary: Queries inside queries, common table expressions and CASE.

sections.p: A query in brackets can be used inside another one. A subquery that gives one value can sit anywhere a value can, such as a comparison with the average. One that gives a column can be used with IN.
sections.out:
nut | count
beechnut | 20
acorn | 12

name
Acorn
Bramble
Hazel

sections.p: WITH name AS (...) names a query, called a common table expression, that the main query can then use like a table. It lets you build a long query in readable steps. CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END picks a value row by row, like an if in other languages.
sections.code:
WITH totals AS (
    SELECT squirrel_id, SUM(count) AS nuts
    FROM stashes
    GROUP BY squirrel_id
)
SELECT s.name,
       COALESCE(t.nuts, 0) AS nuts,
       CASE
           WHEN t.nuts >= 20 THEN 'ready for winter'
           WHEN t.nuts >= 5 THEN 'getting there'
           ELSE 'needs help'
       END AS status
FROM squirrels AS s
LEFT JOIN totals AS t ON t.squirrel_id = s.id
ORDER BY nuts DESC, s.name;
sections.out:
name | nuts | status
Bramble | 27 | ready for winter
Hazel | 21 | ready for winter
Acorn | 3 | needs help
Pip | 2 | needs help
Rowan | 0 | needs help

practice.code:
SELECT kind FROM trees
WHERE height_m = (SELECT MAX(height_m) FROM trees);
practice.why: The subquery finds the greatest height, 30.0, and the outer query finds the tree with that height.

practice.code:
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN born < 2023 THEN 'elder' ELSE 'young' END AS age_group
FROM squirrels
WHERE id <= 2;
options:
name | age_group
Hazel | elder
Acorn | young

name | age_group
Hazel | young
Acorn | elder

name | age_group
Hazel | elder
Acorn | elder
practice.answer:
name | age_group
Hazel | elder
Acorn | young
practice.why: Hazel was born in 2022, before 2023. Acorn was born in 2024.

lessons.title: Views
lessons.summary: Named queries you can SELECT from like a table.

sections.p: A VIEW stores a query under a name. Afterwards you SELECT from it as if it were a table. The data still lives in the real tables; the view just remembers the question. Views are handy when the same join or grouping appears in several places.
sections.out:
tree | residents
oak | 2
beech | 1
hazel | 1
ash | 0

tree
ash

sections.p: A view can hide a multi-table join behind a simple name. Here each stash line gains the squirrel's name and tree. Filtering the view feels like filtering one wide table.
sections.code:
CREATE VIEW stash_labels AS
SELECT s.name AS squirrel, t.kind AS tree, st.nut, st.count
FROM stashes AS st
JOIN squirrels AS s ON s.id = st.squirrel_id
JOIN trees AS t ON t.id = s.tree_id;

SELECT squirrel, nut, count FROM stash_labels
WHERE tree = 'oak'
ORDER BY count DESC;
sections.out:
squirrel | nut | count
Hazel | acorn | 12
Hazel | hazelnut | 5
Hazel | beechnut | 4
Acorn | acorn | 3

sections.p: DROP VIEW removes a view (not the underlying data). CREATE VIEW again installs a new definition. In SQLite, replacing a view is drop-then-create.
sections.out:
nut | total
acorn | 22
beechnut | 24

nut | stashes
acorn | 3
beechnut | 2
hazelnut | 2

practice.why: Oak is 21.5 and beech is 30.0; ORDER BY kind puts beech first.

practice.q: What happens to the table data when you DROP VIEW tree_residents?
options: The view disappears; the trees and squirrels tables stay
practice.answer: The view disappears; the trees and squirrels tables stay
practice.why: A view is only a stored query, not a copy of the rows.
The three acorn stashes hold 12, 3 and 7.

lessons.title: Window functions
lessons.summary: ROW_NUMBER, SUM OVER and RANK without collapsing rows.

sections.p: A window function computes a value from related rows while still returning every row. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) numbers rows inside each group, and SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ...) repeats the group total on each line. Unlike GROUP BY, the detail rows stay visible.
sections.code:
SELECT s.name,
       st.nut,
       st.count,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY st.squirrel_id ORDER BY st.count DESC) AS rank_in_stash,
       SUM(st.count) OVER (PARTITION BY st.squirrel_id) AS squirrel_total
FROM stashes AS st
JOIN squirrels AS s ON s.id = st.squirrel_id
ORDER BY s.name, rank_in_stash;
sections.out:
name | nut | count | rank_in_stash | squirrel_total
Acorn | acorn | 3 | 1 | 3
Bramble | beechnut | 20 | 1 | 27
Bramble | acorn | 7 | 2 | 27
Hazel | acorn | 12 | 1 | 21
Hazel | hazelnut | 5 | 2 | 21
Hazel | beechnut | 4 | 3 | 21
Pip | hazelnut | 2 | 1 | 2

sections.p: An ORDER BY inside OVER without PARTITION BY walks the whole result in that order. SUM(nuts) OVER (ORDER BY nuts DESC, name) is a running total down the ranked list.
sections.code:
SELECT name, nuts,
       SUM(nuts) OVER (ORDER BY nuts DESC, name) AS running
FROM (
    SELECT s.name, COALESCE(SUM(st.count), 0) AS nuts
    FROM squirrels AS s
    LEFT JOIN stashes AS st ON st.squirrel_id = s.id
    GROUP BY s.id
)
ORDER BY nuts DESC, name;
sections.out:
name | nuts | running
Bramble | 27 | 27
Hazel | 21 | 48
Acorn | 3 | 51
Pip | 2 | 53
Rowan | 0 | 53

sections.p: RANK() leaves gaps after ties; ROW_NUMBER() never ties. Both need an ORDER BY in the window. Here squirrels are ranked by how many stashes they have.
sections.code:
SELECT s.name,
       COUNT(st.id) AS stashes,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(st.id) DESC) AS place
FROM squirrels AS s
LEFT JOIN stashes AS st ON st.squirrel_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id
ORDER BY place, s.name;
sections.out:
name | stashes | place
Hazel | 3 | 1
Bramble | 2 | 2
Acorn | 1 | 3
Pip | 1 | 3
Rowan | 0 | 5

practice.code:
SELECT kind,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY height_m DESC) AS n
FROM trees
WHERE height_m IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY n;
practice.why: Beech is tallest, then oak, then hazel. Ash has NULL height and is filtered out.

practice.q: How does SUM(count) OVER (PARTITION BY squirrel_id) differ from GROUP BY squirrel_id?
options: The window keeps one result row per stash; GROUP BY collapses to one row per squirrel
PARTITION BY only works with AVG
practice.answer: The window keeps one result row per stash; GROUP BY collapses to one row per squirrel
practice.why: That is the point of window functions: aggregates beside the detail.

practice.code:
SELECT nut, count,
       SUM(count) OVER (PARTITION BY nut) AS nut_total
FROM stashes
WHERE nut = 'hazelnut'
ORDER BY count;
practice.why: Both hazelnut rows share the partition total 2 + 5 = 7.

lessons.title: Transactions
lessons.summary: BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK so a group of changes lands together.

sections.p: A transaction groups statements so they either all happen or none do. BEGIN starts one, COMMIT makes the changes permanent, and ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN. That matters when two updates must stay in step: you never want only one of them saved.
sections.out:
kind | height_m
ash | 8.5

name
Nutmeg

sections.p: If something goes wrong — or you change your mind — ROLLBACK restores the tables to how they were at BEGIN. Here every stash is deleted inside a transaction, then the delete is undone.
sections.out:
mid
0

after
7

sections.p: Until you COMMIT, other connections would not see your changes (and in these lessons each example is its own connection anyway). Rolling back after a failed idea leaves the sample data untouched for the next query in the same script only if you opened a transaction — without BEGIN, each statement is its own tiny transaction.
sections.out:
before
5

after
5

practice.why: ROLLBACK undoes the UPDATE, so oak is still 21.5.
Three acorn rows are deleted and committed, leaving four stashes.

options: Makes the changes since BEGIN permanent
practice.answer: Makes the changes since BEGIN permanent
practice.why: COMMIT ends the transaction by keeping its writes.

lessons.title: Project: a winter-readiness report
lessons.summary: WITH, joins, CASE and RANK on the sample squirrel world.

sections.p: Winter readiness means enough nuts buried before the cold. This report builds totals per squirrel with a WITH clause, joins each total to its tree, labels a status with CASE, and ranks everyone with RANK(). Rowan has no tree and no stashes, so the tree shows as none and the status as short.
sections.code:
WITH totals AS (
    SELECT s.id AS squirrel_id, s.name, s.tree_id,
           COALESCE(SUM(st.count), 0) AS nuts
    FROM squirrels AS s
    LEFT JOIN stashes AS st ON st.squirrel_id = s.id
    GROUP BY s.id
),
readiness AS (
    SELECT t.name,
           COALESCE(tr.kind, 'none') AS tree,
           t.nuts,
           CASE
               WHEN t.nuts >= 20 THEN 'ready'
               WHEN t.nuts >= 5 THEN 'almost'
               ELSE 'short'
           END AS status,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY t.nuts DESC, t.name) AS place
    FROM totals AS t
    LEFT JOIN trees AS tr ON tr.id = t.tree_id
)
SELECT place, name, tree, nuts, status
FROM readiness
ORDER BY place;
sections.out:
place | name | tree | nuts | status
1 | Bramble | beech | 27 | ready
2 | Hazel | oak | 21 | ready
3 | Acorn | oak | 3 | short
4 | Pip | hazel | 2 | short
5 | Rowan | none | 0 | short

sections.p: Add a view that stores the readiness query, filter to only short squirrels who still need help, or join stash nut kinds so the report shows each squirrel's favourite nut.

practice.q: Why use LEFT JOIN trees in the readiness step?
options: So squirrels with no tree_id still appear, with a NULL tree filled by COALESCE
INNER JOIN is not allowed inside WITH
practice.answer: So squirrels with no tree_id still appear, with a NULL tree filled by COALESCE
practice.why: Rowan has tree_id NULL; an inner join would drop that row.
Hazel has 21 and Bramble has 27.

practice.code:
SELECT COALESCE(kind, 'none') AS tree
FROM (SELECT NULL AS kind)
UNION ALL
SELECT kind FROM trees WHERE id = 2;
practice.why: COALESCE turns NULL into none, then the hazel row is appended.
